title: 16. Shell Scripting
content:
# 16. Shell Scripting

Shell scripts are excellent for orchestration, glue code, administration, and short automation. They become fragile when used as a replacement for a general-purpose language without need.

## A reliable starting point

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

main() {
    printf 'Hello, %s\n' "${1:-world}"
}

main "$@"
```

`set -euo pipefail` improves failure visibility but has important Bash semantics. Learn the exceptions rather than treating it as magic.

## Variables and quoting

```bash
name="Ada"
printf '%s\n' "$name"
```

Quote variables by default:

```bash
rm -- "$file"
```

Unquoted expansions can undergo word splitting and pathname expansion.

## Arguments

```bash
printf 'script=%s\n' "$0"
printf 'first=%s\n' "${1:-}"
printf 'count=%s\n' "$#"
printf 'all=%s\n' "$*"
printf 'each=%s\n' "$@"
```

When forwarding arguments, use:

```bash
some_command "$@"
```

## Conditionals

```bash
if [[ -f "$file" ]]; then
    printf 'regular file\n'
else
    printf 'not a regular file\n'
fi
```

`[[ ... ]]` is Bash syntax. POSIX `sh` uses `[ ... ]`.

## Loops

```bash
for file in ./*.log; do
    [ -e "$file" ] || continue
    printf '%s\n' "$file"
done
```

## Functions and exit status

```bash
check_config() {
    test -f /etc/myapp/config
}
```

Functions return the status of their last command unless you explicitly `return`.

## Temporary files

Avoid predictable filenames for sensitive temporary data. Use `mktemp` where available:

```bash
tmp=$(mktemp)
trap 'rm -f "$tmp"' EXIT
```

## ShellCheck

Validate scripts:

```bash
bash -n script.sh
shellcheck script.sh
```

## When not to use shell

Use Python, Go, Node.js, or another language when you need complex data structures, extensive error handling, APIs, concurrency, or large application logic.

## Practice

Write a script that accepts a directory, validates it, counts regular files, reports failures, and exits non-zero for invalid input. Test it with spaces in the directory name.
